newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African unions reject accord to end sugar strike.
newsitem.headline: S.African unions reject accord to end sugar strike.

text.p: A draft agreement to end a 17-day-old strike by thousands of South African sugar workers was rejected by unions who will now approach a national labour dispute resolution body, union spokesmen said on Thursday.
Some 4,000 workers have brought production to a halt at 14 mills and refineries operated by Ilovo Sugar Ltd and Tongaat-Hulett Ltd since July 2, to back their wage demands.

A draft agreement reached earlier this week to raise wages by 11.5 percent backdated to April 1 was rejected by workers, union spokesman Eric Botha said, adding that the unions will now approach the Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration (CCA) to help end the strike.

"There was no signing (of the draft agreement) because our guys rejected the proposal. There are no more negotiations and we have decided to approach the CCMA today (Thursday) to help us settle this," Botha said.
"The signing is off, things are not moving," said Bheki Sibiya, a spokesman for the two companies.

Labour Minister Tito Mboweni said last month the CCMA had achieved an 86 percent success rate nationally since it was set up in late 1996 in terms of the new Labour Relations Act (LRA) to provide quick and fair mediation in labour disputes.
Delegates who attended Thursday's meeting of the five unions representing the workers, said five of the 14 mills and refineries had been willing to accept the offer.
But they would not return to work, another union official said.
"The majority of the mills say no, so those five will not go back to work," said Lawrence Nsibande.
The mills are Illovo's Sezela and Tongaat's Felixston, Entumeni, Amatikulu and Pongola.
"The situation is very bad at the moment because workers' expectations were very high after the companies predicted that this would be a record crop. The workers want a good increase," he added.
The current season's production was estimated to be a record 2.5 million tonnes, with 48 percent being exported for the 1997/98 season rising from 44 percent in the 1996/97 period.
Overall exports earnings are expected to be 1,462 billion rand which was an increase of 271 million rand over last season.
Sugar industry sources have said production of 83,500 tonnes of cane per day was being lost, but they have declined to put a value on the figure.
To make up for lost production the crushing season will be extended into late December, the source said. The normal season lasts from April to mid-December.
